newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour keeps lead despite tax fear-Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour keeps lead despite tax fear-Reuters poll.

text.p: Britain's Labour opposition has still not shed its image as the party of high taxes but this will not deter voters from electing it to office with a commanding lead over the Conservatives, a poll for Reuters showed on Tuesday.

The pre-election survey of 1,049 voters across Britain by research organisation NOP put support, among those expressing a preference, at 50 percent for Labour compared with 30 percent for the Conservatives.
The Liberal Democrats polled 14 percent and other parties six percent -- including two percent for the Referendum Party of Sir James Goldsmith.
British voters would prefer to wait and see on European monetary union rather than plunging in at the start of a single currency in 1999, the poll showed.
The survey found 41 percent wanted Britain to see how the proposed single currency worked in action before deciding whether to join.
Some 30 percent said the country should stay out altogether.

The poll is the first of a series that NOP is conducting for Reuters, the global news and information group, in the run-up to the election, which must be held by May 22 but is widely expected to take place on May 1.
All political parties tend to play down the significance of opinion polls, remembering how they failed to predict the Conservatives' victory at the 1992 general election.
Nevertheless, the Reuters/NOP survey will be a blow to Prime Minister John Major, who has been waiting in vain for Britain's robust economic recovery to revive his party's popularity.

Major, his party deeply divided over Europe, is bracing for further disappointment on Thursday in a by-election for the seat of Wirral South in northwest England left vacant by the death of Conservative member of parliament Barry Porter.
Wirral South has been a safe Conservative seat since it was created in 1983, but polls suggest it will fall to Labour, giving the party a flying start for the national election campaign.

Labour leader Tony Blair will be concerned that voters are still suspicious of his party when it comes to tax -- despite his pledge not to raise income tax rates for the five-year life of the next parliament if Labour wins power.
In the Reuters/NOP poll, 32 percent of those questioned felt total taxes would be higher under a Labour government compared with 19 percent who felt they would pay more under the Conservatives.
The ruling party and Labour came out fairly closely on the critical question of who can be trusted to run the economy. Conservative polled 32 percent against Labour's 30 percent.
The polling organisation conducted face-to-face interviews on Friday, February 21, with 1,049 voters in 51 parliamentary constituencies.
The results of the survey are in line with other opinion polls since the start of the year.
These have shown Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979, ahead of the Conservatives by 15 to 25 percentage points.
The Reuters/NOP poll showed support for Labour fairly evenly distributed between the sexes and among age groups.
Among men, 53 percent said they were most inclined to back Labour and 26 percent opted for the Conservatives. The figures for women were 50 percent and 32 percent respectively.

The 18-34 age group split 57 percent for Labour against 24 percent for the Conservatives. Those aged 35-54 divided 48 percent for Labour and 28 percent for the ruling party, and among those 55 or older 51 percent expressed a preference for Labour against 33 percent for Conservatives.
On Europe, the poll gave Labour a slight edge, with 34 percent of respondents trusting it most to represent Britain's interests against 31 percent for the Conservatives.
